title: Proof Systems for QBF Synthesis: Extracting Skolem and Herbrand Functions
abstract: Strategy extraction in QBF proof systems usually attempts to extract winning strategies from valid proofs. However, an alternative (and arguably more powerful) view is to extract Skolem/Herbrand functions, or equivalently synthesis of the game values at all intermediate points. In this paper, we investigate the existence and properties of such proof systems from which one can extract Skolem and Herbrand functions. We propose such a proof system for QBF, which we show is sound and complete, and from which extraction of Skolem/Herbrand functions can be performed, and game values computed, in polynomial time. We also show that this system is optimal among all proof systems that allow efficient extraction of Skolem/Herbrand functions. We provide conditional lower bound results for our new proof system and compare it to several existing/standard proof systems for QBF that have been studied in the literature, showing interesting orthogonality results. Finally, we provide a compilation algorithm that takes an arbitrary QBF and synthesizes a proof in our system, from which Skolem and Herbrand functions can be easily computed.

      Abstract
Strategy extraction in QBF proof systems usually attempts to extract winning strategies from valid
proofs. However, an alternative (and arguably more powerful) view is to extract Skolem/Herbrand
functions, or equivalently synthesis of the game values at all intermediate points. In this paper, we
investigate the existence and properties of such proof systems from which one can extract Skolem
and Herbrand functions. We propose such a proof system for QBF, which we show is sound and
complete, and from which extraction of Skolem/Herbrand functions can be performed, and game
values computed, in polynomial time. We also show that this system is optimal among all proof
systems that allow efficient extraction of Skolem/Herbrand functions. We provide conditional lower
bound results for our new proof system and compare it to several existing/standard proof systems
for QBF that have been studied in the literature, showing interesting orthogonality results. Finally,
we provide a compilation algorithm that takes an arbitrary QBF and synthesizes a proof in our
system, from which Skolem and Herbrand functions can be easily computed.

 1      Introduction
Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBF) extend propositional logic with universal and existential
quantification over Boolean variables, providing a natural and expressive framework for
modelling problems with alternation of choices. This expressiveness makes QBF a suitable
formalism for a range of applications in logic and artificial intelligence [20,48]. QBFs are widely
used in formal verification and planning, where they arise in bounded and unbounded model
checking, automated synthesis, and reasoning about systems and games with adversarial
or environmental behaviour (see [48] for a survey). QBFs also play an important role in

      knowledge representation and reasoning, including belief revision, non-monotonic reasoning,
      and reasoning under uncertainty. Due to their PSPACE-completeness, QBFs serve both as
      a practical modelling tool for complex reasoning tasks and as a theoretical benchmark for
      studying the limits of automated reasoning techniques. One is often interested in not simply
      deciding the satisfiability of a QBF, but also in obtaining a certificate for this answer that
      can be independently verified. Such a certificate is typically a formal proof of truth or falsity
      of the formula in a specific proof system.

          When a QBF encodes a two-player game, an equally important task is to synthesize a
      winning strategy for each player – whenever such a strategy exists – from any intermediate
      state that may arise after a partial sequence of moves. In many games, a player cannot
      guarantee victory against all possible responses of the opponent. Nevertheless, if the opponent
      makes a suboptimal move, the player may still be able to exploit it and steer the game towards
      a win. Automatically synthesizing such “win-whenever-possible” strategies for both players
      is therefore valuable, since the opponent’s behaviour is generally unknown a priori. As we
      argue in this paper, synthesizing strategies that enable each player to win whenever possible
      from states reached after partial play corresponds to extracting Herbrand functions for the
      universal player and Skolem functions for the existential player from the underlying QBF.
      This perspective highlights the importance of extracting both Herbrand and Skolem functions
      from a given QBF, regardless of whether the formula is true. Notably, this departs from the
      prevailing treatment in the literature e.g., in [6, 7, 17, 37, 42], where instead of Herbrand and
      Skolem functions, the only extracted objects are winning strategies, for universal variables
      in false QBFs and for existential variables in true QBFs. A closely related line of work
      appears in Boolean functional synthesis [2–4, 25, 31–33, 38, 47], which has largely focused on
      synthesizing Skolem functions when the specification is given as a QBF with a ∀∗ ∃∗ prefix.

          Given their theoretical and practical importance, a long line of work has emerged on proof
      systems for QBF solvers [8, 10, 15, 21, 22, 28, 39, 44, 45]. Examples include resolution-based
      systems such as Q-resolution [40] and its variants [30, 51], as well as systems based on
      expansion [17, 35], dependency schemes [12, 44, 50], and clause learning [13, 23, 24]. Studying
      proof systems for QBF enables a precise comparison between different solving paradigms and
      provides insights into the kinds of reasoning that can or cannot be efficiently simulated [13,
      34,35,49]. Proofs also serve as certificates of realizability or unrealizability: a proof of validity
      implicitly encodes winning strategies, while a refutation can certify the absence of any correct
      winning strategy. Several approaches use QBF proof systems to extract winning strategies,
      often in the form of circuits [6, 11, 15, 17].

          It is useful at this point to clarify that, in our view, there is some inconsistency in the
      literature as to the usage of the terms Skolem functions and existential winning strategies
      (and likewise Herbrand functions and universal winning strategies). In many papers these
      terms are just used synonymously. However, as we try to point out here, these notions are
      fundamentally different. Skolem functions solve a much harder problem than just computing
      an existential winning strategy (they also do that): they provide “win-whenever-possible”
      strategies, as explained above. This is in line with their definition used in standard texts on
      logic [26, 41] and Skolem synthesis [1]. To informally illustrate this point with an example
      (formal examples are given in Example 3.3 and in Lemma 5.1): when playing chess (which
      gives rise to interesting QBFs [46]): a winning strategy (e.g. for white) would determine a
      sequence of winning moves for white from the standard initial configuration, while a Skolem
      function (again for white) would specify a sequence of winning moves for white starting from
      any game position, provided that a win for white is still possible at this point.

Our contributions. In this paper, we investigate the existence and properties of proof
systems for QBF synthesis that allow the efficient extraction of both Skolem and Herbrand
functions, representing “win-whenever-possible” strategies of the existential and universal
player respectively, for all QBFs. Our contributions are the following:

   We present a new proof system SynQBF (the name refers to Synthesis QBF) that is
   complete for both false and true QBFs. We show that SynQBF provides a certificate for
   the game value of a QBF viewed as a two-player game, not only after all moves have
   been played by the respective players, but after any partial play.
   Notably, this proof system can handle arbitrary prenex QBFs, not just those where the
   matrix is in conjunctive normal form.
   We show that SynQBF proofs admit polynomial-time extraction of Skolem and Herbrand
   functions, regardless of the truth value (or game value) of the formula. Thus, these
   functions serve as “win-whenever-possible” strategies of the existential and universal
   player, respectively.
   We provide complexity results showing optimality of the SynQBF proof system. More
   precisely, we show that if there is a proof system that can allow polynomial-time extraction
   of both Skolem and Herbrand functions, then our proof system p-simulates it (i.e., every
   proof in that system can be transformed into a proof in our system in polynomial-time).
   We relate our proof system to known proof systems, namely Q-eFrege and Q-Res and show
   simulation and conditional (in)comparability results leading to the situation depicted in
   Figure 1. Interestingly and perhaps surprisingly, SynQBF turns out to be incomparable
   to the rather weak system Q-Res (and in fact even tree-like Q-Res). Intuitively, this is
   due to the fact that SynQBF has to solve a much harder problem, i.e. Skolem/Herbrand
   function synthesis, than Q-Res, which only provides universal winning strategies. Both
   systems are simulated by the strong system Q-eFrege.
   Finally, we provide an algorithm for synthesizing SynQBF proofs from prenex normal
   form QBFs. While in worst case, our algorithm cannot avoid being exponential (if
   PSPACE ̸⊆ P/poly; due to known lower bounds), it is counter-example driven, and paves
   the way for potential practical algorithms towards knowledge compilation for synthesis
   from QBFs.

    The structure of the paper is as follows. We start with preliminaries in Section 2, followed
by Section 3, where we provide the basic definition of winning strategies and Skolem/Herbrand
functions, and highlight the differences between them. In Section 4, we introduce our new
proof system. We show that it is sound and complete, and that it allows for efficient extraction
of Skolem and Herbrand functions, as well as provide complexity bounds and optimality
results. In Section 5 we show the relationship of our proof system with earlier systems. We
provide an algorithm for automatically synthesizing proofs in our proof system in Section 6,
and conclude in Section 7.

       2     Preliminaries
      For n ∈ N, we use [n] to denote the set {1, . . . , n}. We assume familiarity with basic notions
      from computational complexity, cf. [5], as well as from logic, cf. [41], but define all specific
      concepts needed in this paper.
          We consider propositional formulas φ built from constants 0, 1, connectors ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔,
      and propositional variables. Similarly, a propositional circuit C is built from the same
      components as a formula, differing in the underlying structure: In formulas, every internal
      node may only be used once, while in circuits, they are allowed to be reused [52]. P/poly is
      the class of functions computed by polynomial-size circuits. A literal is a variable v or its
      negation ¬v. A clause is a disjunction of literals, and a formula is in Conjunctive Normal
      Form (CNF) if it is a conjunction of clauses. When V is a set of variables, a (partial)
      assignment to V is a (partial) function α : V → {0, 1}. We write ⟨V ⟩ for the set of all
      complete assignments to V , and vars(φ) or vars(α) for the set of all variables occurring
      in φ or α (i.e. variables assigned truth values by α). If V = {x1 , . . . , xn } we also write
      ⟨x1 , . . . , xn ⟩ for ⟨V ⟩. We denote by φ|α the formula φ where each variable v ∈ vars(α) has
      been substituted by α(v).


      Quantified Boolean Formulas. A (closed prenex) Quantified Boolean Formula (QBF) is a
      formula Q.φ where φ is a propositional formula and Q is the quantifier prefix that quantifies
      all variables v in φ either existentially as ∃v or universally as ∀v.
          Whether a QBF is true or not can be defined recursively. The formula ∀u Q.φ is true if
      both Q.φ|u=0 and Q.φ|u=1 are true. The formula ∃x Q.φ is true if at least one of Q.φ|u=0
      and Q.φ|u=1 is true.
          In a fully quantified prenex QBF, the quantifier prefix determines a total order of the
      variables. Given a variable v, we will sometimes refer to the variables preceding v in the
      prefix as variables left of v; analogously we speak of the variables right of v.
          A QBF Q1 x1 . . . Qk xk .φ can be seen as a game between two players: universal (∀) and
      existential (∃). In the i-th step of the game, the player Qi assigns a value to the variable xi .
      The existential player wins if φ evaluates to 1 under the assignment constructed in the game.
      The universal player wins if φ evaluates to 0.


      Proof systems. According to [29], a proof system for a language L is a polynomial-time
      onto function P : {0, 1}∗ → L. Each string φ ∈ L is a theorem and if P (π) = φ, then π
      is a proof of φ in P (a P -proof). Given a polynomial-time function P : {0, 1}∗ → {0, 1}∗
      the fact that P ({0, 1}∗ ) ⊆ L is the soundness of P and the fact that P ({0, 1}∗ ) ⊇ L is the
      completeness of P . A proof system P1 p-simulates a different proof system P2 , if every P2
      proof can be transformed into a P1 proof of the same theorem in polynomial-time.

       4     A new proof system designed for QBF synthesis
      In this section, we will define our new proof system and show its properties.

      4.1    Proof system definition
      When talking about strategy extraction in QBF proof systems, earlier work has focused on
      efficiently extracting a winning strategy (for the existential or universal player, depending on
      whether the formula is true or false) from proofs (cf. e.g. [6, 15, 30]). Here, we introduce a
      new proof system, which can do more than that: Given a proof, we are able to extract both
      Skolem and Herbrand functions for the existential and universal player, respectively.
           For the definition of the proof system, we first need to introduce the notion of represent-
      ability and some notations which are used throughout this section.

      ▶ Definition 4.1. For a gate type ⊗ ∈ {∨, ∧}, a circuit φ, and two distinct variables x, y ∈
      vars(φ), we say that “φ is ⊗-representable for x, y” if φ|x=y=b ↔ (φ|x=0,y=1 ⊗ φ|x=1,y=0 ),
      where b = 1 if ⊗ = ∨, and b = 0 otherwise.

         For instance, φ = (x1 ∨ x3 ) ∧ (¬x2 ∨ ¬x1 ) is ∧-representable for x1 , x2 since with b = 0,
      φ|x1 =x2 =0 = x3 ↔ (φ|x1 =0,x2 =1 ∧ φ|x1 =1,x2 =0 ). But it is not ∨-representable for x1 , x2 since
      with b = 1, we can see that φ|x1 =x2 =1 = 0 but φ|x1 =0,x2 =1 ∨ φ|x1 =1,x2 =0 = 1.

 7     Conclusion
In this paper, we clarified the difference between winning strategies and Skolem/Herbrand
functions of QBFs, and introduced a new proof system called SynQBF. Our proof system
allows us to extract both Skolem and Herbrand functions for the existential and universal
player respectively, in time polynomial in the proof size, regardless of whether the QBF is
true or false. This also allows us to obtain circuits for game values after all partial plays of
the game. We show that our proof system is optimal and provide conditional lower bound
results, and also relate this to existing/standard proof systems for QBF in the literature. As
future work, we would like to implement our proof construction algorithm and show practical
utility of our framework. We also hope that this work will lead to more attention towards
win-whenever-possible strategies in QBF, and their computation.
